name: Adrenosterone (11-keto-androstenedione)
lead: Adrenosterone, also called 11-ketoandrostenedione, 11-oxoandrostenedione or Reichstein's substance G, is a steroid made in the adrenal glands. Tadeus Reichstein first isolated it from the adrenal cortex in 1936.[1] It has very weak androgenic activity on its own and is an intermediate and prohormone of 11-ketotestosterone.[1]

Since about 2007 it has been sold as a dietary supplement (often under the name 11-OXO) marketed for fat loss and muscle gain. Proponents attribute this to inhibition of 11β-HSD1, the enzyme that converts cortisone to cortisol, which would reduce cortisol activity; Wikipedia presents this as a proposed mechanism.[1]

No human clinical trial of adrenosterone supplements for body composition was found. Published work covers analytical detection for doping control and the role of 11-oxygenated androgens in conditions such as polycystic ovary syndrome.[1][2][3]

paras: Adrenosterone has the formula C19H24O3, a molar mass of about 300 g/mol and a melting point of 222 degrees Celsius; its systematic name is androst-4-ene-3,11,17-trione [1]. It carries a ketone group at the 11 position, which distinguishes it from androstenedione, and Wikipedia describes its androgenic effect as extremely weak [1]. Other names include Reichstein's substance G, 11-KA4 and 11-OXO [1].

Tadeus Reichstein isolated the compound from the adrenal cortex at the University of Basel in 1936, which is why it carries his name in older literature [1]. A 1967 paper in Steroids described its metabolism [6]. In the 2000s it moved from steroid chemistry into the supplement market, where it has been sold since about 2007 under names such as 11-OXO for fat loss and muscle gain [1].

It occurs in trace amounts in humans and most mammals and in larger amounts in fish.[1] It is thought to act as a competitive, selective inhibitor of 11β-HSD1, an enzyme that regenerates cortisol from cortisone, though this is described as a proposed mechanism rather than an established one.[1]
Analytical work has characterised its metabolism, including fungal biotransformation, and multi-class steroid assays include related adrenal steroids.[4][5]

In biology the compound is an intermediate in the pathway to 11-ketotestosterone, an androgen that is the principal androgen in fish, where adrenosterone is found in larger amounts [1]. In humans, 11-oxygenated androgens as a class are now studied as contributors to androgen excess in polycystic ovary syndrome, and two registered studies examine their effect on metabolic dysfunction and muscle insulin sensitivity [2][3].

Wikipedia reports that it has been sold as a supplement since 2007 for fat loss and muscle gain, with the marketing rationale based on blocking cortisol activation to limit muscle breakdown.[1] Doping-control researchers have published criteria for detecting its use.[1] It also serves as a synthesis intermediate for other steroids such as fluoxymesterone.[1]

The World Anti-Doping Agency's Prohibited List includes adrenosterone. A 2024 paper reports that use can be detected by monitoring the urinary metabolites 11-beta-hydroxyandrosterone and 11-beta-hydroxyetiocholanolone, and proposes 11-ketotestosterone as an additional target analyte for doping controls [7]. Wikipedia also notes that the compound serves as an intermediate in industrial synthesis of fluoxymesterone and, through an RTI International process, dimethandrolone [1].

No studies found for its use as a fat-loss or muscle supplement. Registered trials (status unknown) are examining 11-oxygenated androgens, a class that includes this compound, in women with polycystic ovary syndrome, in relation to skeletal muscle insulin sensitivity and metabolic dysfunction.[2][3]

The two registered studies are an observational-style trial of 20 participants (DIMOXIS, started 2022) and a study of 100 women with PCOS (started 2021); both list their status as unknown [2][3]. Neither tests adrenosterone supplements for appearance.

timeline.event: Isolated from the adrenal cortex by Tadeus Reichstein.[1]
Begins to be sold as a dietary supplement for fat loss and muscle gain.[1]

card.summary: An adrenal steroid sold as '11-OXO' for fat loss via cortisol blocking; the pitch rests on a proposed mechanism with no supplement trials.
card.note: Doping-control methods exist to detect its use.

quick.overview:
Adrenosterone is a natural adrenal steroid that has been sold since about 2007 as a fat-loss and muscle supplement.
No human trial has tested it for that purpose.
quick.mechanism: It is proposed to inhibit 11β-HSD1, the enzyme that makes cortisol from cortisone, and it is a precursor to 11-ketotestosterone. Its direct androgen activity is described as extremely weak.
quick.risks: No supplement safety data from trials were found. Anti-doping labs have developed ways to detect it.

chain: Proposed to block cortisol regeneration by 11-beta-HSD1
Less cortisol activity is claimed to mean less fat and less muscle breakdown
angle.text: Adrenosterone is sold as a fat-loss and muscle-gain supplement. The marketing explanation is that blocking the enzyme that turns cortisone into active cortisol lowers cortisol's muscle-wasting and fat-storing effects, which would show up as a leaner physique.
